section_content: When a ball leaves the hand at an angle to the ground, two things happen at once. Horizontally it just keeps gliding at whatever sideways speed it started with, because no force pushes it forward or backward. Vertically it slows down, stops for an instant, and then falls back under gravity at 9.8 m/s². Combine the two and the path you trace out is a parabola. A stone thrown at 60° above the horizontal at 20 m/s lands roughly 35 m away after about 3.5 s in the air. Drawing the curved flight path with the launch angle, peak, and landing point all on one diagram is what makes the geometry click.
section_title: Throwing a Ball at an Angle
subject: physics
rationale: Section is about projectile flight at an angle; library has a 60-degree trajectory diagram.

section_content: Suppose set A holds the students who play football and set B holds the students who play cricket. The collection of students who play at least one of the two sports is found by gathering everyone in A together with everyone in B, but counting each name only once. We use the symbol ∪ for this combine-without-duplicates operation. If A has 12 members and B has 9, and 4 students play both sports, then the combined group has 12 + 9 − 4 = 17 students. The clearest way to see what's happening is two overlapping circles where the entire shaded region represents the combined set.
subject: math
rationale: Describes set union with overlap counting; library has a union Venn diagram.

section_content: When a cyclist accelerates from rest at a steady 2 m/s², her speed grows by exactly 2 m/s every second. After 1 s she's moving at 2 m/s, after 2 s at 4 m/s, after 3 s at 6 m/s. Plot speed against time and the points fall on a straight line that climbs through the origin with slope 2. That slope is the acceleration itself. If she had started already moving at 3 m/s, the line would still climb at the same rate but would now cross the vertical axis at 3 m/s instead of zero. The shape stays linear as long as the acceleration stays constant.
subject: physics
rationale: Velocity-time linear graph for constant acceleration; library has the UAM v-t image.

section_content: A pairing rule from set X to set Y is called perfect when every member of X is matched with exactly one member of Y, every member of Y is hit by exactly one arrow from X, and no two arrows from X land on the same target. In other words there are no duplicates and nothing is left out on either side. The cleanest way to test this is to draw the two sets as columns of dots and join matched pairs with arrows: a perfect pairing produces a clean one-to-one fan with no orphans on the right and no collisions on the left. Inverses exist exactly for these pairings.
subject: math
rationale: Describes bijection (one-to-one + onto) via arrow visualization; library has it.

section_content: A coin flicked straight up rises, stops for a fraction of a second at the top, and then falls back. Throughout the entire flight gravity pulls it down at 9.8 m/s² — the acceleration never changes sign or magnitude. What does change sign is the velocity. On the way up the velocity points upward but is shrinking. At the peak it equals zero. On the way down it grows again, but now pointing downward. Plot velocity against time, treating up as positive, and you get a single straight line crossing the time axis at the peak. The crossing point marks the instant the coin reverses direction.
subject: physics
rationale: Velocity-time graph for free fall with sign change at peak; library has it.

section_content: Take the three-element set S = {a, b, c}. How many subsets does it have? The empty set counts as one, the three singletons {a}, {b}, {c} are three more, the three pairs {a,b}, {a,c}, {b,c} bring the total to seven, and the whole set S itself rounds it out to eight — in general 2^n for an n-element set. Now order these eight subsets by inclusion: the empty set sits at the bottom, the singletons above it, the pairs above those, and the full set at the top. Connect each subset to the ones immediately above and below by inclusion and you get a layered lattice that fits beautifully on a single page.
subject: math
rationale: Describes power-set lattice ordered by inclusion; library has the 3-element Hasse diagram.

section_content: Suppose a stone is launched at 25 m/s at 53° above the horizontal. To analyze the flight we pry the single starting velocity vector apart into two pieces that act independently. The horizontal piece is 25 cos 53° ≈ 15 m/s and stays the same throughout the motion. The vertical piece is 25 sin 53° ≈ 20 m/s and changes under gravity. Drawing the launch arrow as the diagonal of a right triangle with the horizontal leg and vertical leg labelled is the move that turns one hard 2D problem into two easy 1D problems. The angle between the diagonal and the horizontal leg is the launch angle.
subject: physics
rationale: Decomposing launch velocity into horizontal + vertical components; library has it.

section_content: Sometimes you want to apply two transformations one after the other. If g triples a number and f adds 5, then "do g, then feed the result into f" turns the input 4 into f(g(4)) = f(12) = 17. The combined operation is itself a function, written f ∘ g. Visualizing this as a pipeline — input on the left, an arrow into the g-box, an arrow out of the g-box into the f-box, output on the right — makes it obvious that order matters: g ∘ f would feed the input through f first and produce a different answer (in this case 3(4+5) = 27, not 17).
subject: math
rationale: Describes composition with f after g via pipeline visualization; library has it.

section_content: A jogger runs 200 m east, turns around, and runs 150 m back west. The total length of path her feet traced is 350 m — that's the scalar quantity. But if you draw an arrow from her starting point to where she ended up, that arrow is only 50 m long, pointing east. The two numbers measure genuinely different things: one cares about the wiggly path; the other cares only about start-to-end straight-line offset. They coincide only when the motion is in a straight line without reversal. The difference becomes vivid as soon as the trajectory bends or doubles back.
subject: physics
rationale: Distance vs displacement on a curved/reversing path; library has the curved-path diagram.

section_content: Consider two sets: P, the children who own a bicycle, and Q, the children who own a skateboard. To find the children who own both, we keep only those who appear in P and also appear in Q. The symbol for this operation is ∩ — the upside-down U. If P has 18 members, Q has 11, and together their combined roster has 24 distinct names, then |P ∩ Q| = 18 + 11 − 24 = 5 children own both. Drawing the two groups as overlapping circles makes the answer pop: the answer lives in the lens-shaped overlap region in the middle.
subject: math
rationale: Set intersection via overlapping-circles visualization; library has it.

section_content: When ethanol reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid at around 170°C, the acid protonates the hydroxyl group and turns it into a good leaving group, water. A neighbouring C–H bond donates its electrons to form the new π bond as the water molecule departs. The result is ethene plus water. Because the rate-determining step involves the loss of water from a protonated alcohol to give a carbocation intermediate, the overall mechanism is classified as E1. Tertiary alcohols dehydrate fastest because the carbocation they form is the most stable; primary alcohols often follow E2 instead.
subject: chemistry
rationale: Organic mechanism in chemistry; library has zero chemistry entries so cannot match.

section_content: In an electrochemical cell, oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode. The standard hydrogen electrode is assigned a potential of exactly 0.00 V by international agreement, and every other half-cell is measured against it. A zinc electrode dipped into 1 M Zn²⁺ solution and connected to the SHE registers −0.76 V, telling us zinc loses electrons more readily than hydrogen does. The salt bridge keeps the two half-cells electrically neutral by allowing ions to migrate without letting the solutions mix. The cell EMF is the difference between the two electrode potentials.
subject: chemistry
rationale: Electrochemistry concept in chemistry; library has no chemistry entries.

section_content: Photosynthesis splits into two coupled stages. The light-dependent reactions, in the thylakoid membrane, capture photons and use that energy to lift electrons from water to NADP⁺, releasing oxygen as a side-product and pumping protons to drive ATP synthesis. The light-independent reactions, in the stroma, take the ATP and NADPH from the first stage and use them to fix CO₂ into 3-phosphoglycerate via the enzyme RuBisCO. Three turns of the resulting Calvin cycle build one molecule of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, the precursor to glucose. The two stages exchange chemical energy carriers, not light.
subject: biology
rationale: Biology topic; library has no biology entries.

section_content: DNA replication is semi-conservative: each new double helix consists of one parental strand and one freshly synthesised one. The process begins when helicase unwinds the parental duplex at an origin of replication. DNA polymerase III adds nucleotides only in the 5'→3' direction, so on one template strand it works continuously toward the replication fork (the leading strand) while on the other it must work in short fragments backwards (the lagging strand). DNA ligase later seals these Okazaki fragments. Topoisomerase relieves the supercoiling stress that builds up ahead of the fork.
subject: biology
rationale: Cellular biology topic; library has no biology entries.

section_content: The Indian monsoon arises from a seasonal reversal of pressure and wind. In summer, the landmass heats faster than the surrounding ocean, creating a low-pressure zone over the Tibetan Plateau and northern India. Air rushes in from the high-pressure region over the cool Indian Ocean, picking up moisture as it crosses the warm sea surface, and dumps that moisture as it rises against the Western Ghats and the Himalayas. In winter the gradient reverses: cool, dry air flows out from the high-pressure interior toward the warmer ocean, producing the relatively dry north-east monsoon along the Coromandel coast.
subject: geography
rationale: Climatology in geography; library has no geography entries.

section_content: Tectonic plates move because the rocky mantle beneath them flows in slow convection cells driven by heat from the Earth's interior. Where two oceanic plates pull apart, magma rises into the gap and freezes into new sea floor — a mid-ocean ridge. Where an oceanic plate meets a continental one, the denser oceanic slab is forced down beneath the lighter continental crust, melting partially as it descends and feeding chains of volcanoes inland from a deep ocean trench. Where two continental plates collide, neither sinks, and the crust crumples upward into mountain belts like the Himalayas.
subject: geography
rationale: Plate-tectonics topic; library has no geography entries.

section_content: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 18th century because several preconditions converged there earlier than elsewhere: abundant coal close to navigable rivers, a stable Parliament that protected property rights, an Atlantic trade network supplying cotton, and an existing class of merchants with capital to invest. James Watt's improved steam engine of 1769 made coal-fired power portable enough to drive factory machinery; this in turn allowed textile production to migrate from rural cottages to centralised mills along the rivers of Lancashire. By 1850 these conditions had spread to Belgium, France, and the German states.
subject: history
rationale: History topic; library has no history entries.

section_content: The non-cooperation movement, launched by Gandhi in 1920, was the first mass-scale Indian challenge to British rule. Indians were urged to surrender titles, boycott government schools, courts, and council elections, refuse foreign cloth, and resign from the colonial bureaucracy. Within a year the movement had drawn in millions across class and regional lines, paralysing parts of the colonial administration. Gandhi suspended it abruptly in February 1922 after a mob in Chauri Chaura set fire to a police station and killed 22 constables — a turn of violence he refused to countenance from a movement defined by its non-violent discipline.
subject: history
rationale: Modern Indian history; library has no history entries.

section_content: Spanish verbs in the present indicative agree with their subject in person and number through a small set of suffixes attached to the stem. The regular -ar verb hablar (to speak) inflects as hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan across the six person-number slots. The -er verb comer parallels this pattern with -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en, and -ir verbs like vivir use -o, -es, -e, -imos, -ís, -en. Because the suffix already carries person information, the explicit subject pronoun (yo, tú, él) is usually dropped unless contrast or emphasis is needed.
subject: languages
rationale: Linguistics; library has no language entries.

section_content: French nouns carry grammatical gender, and the gender of the noun governs the form of any article or adjective attached to it. Most nouns ending in -tion, -té, -ence, -ie are feminine; those in -ment, -age (when not from a Greek root), -eau, -isme tend to be masculine. There are reliable suffix patterns but also stubborn exceptions: la peau is feminine even though it ends in -eau, and le silence is masculine even though it ends in -ence. Native speakers internalise gender by hearing the article alongside the noun rather than memorising rules in isolation.
subject: languages
rationale: Linguistics; library has no language entries.

section_content: A particle is launched from ground level at 30 m/s at 45° above the horizontal. We model it as moving in two independent dimensions: horizontal motion at constant velocity, and vertical motion under gravity g = 9.8 m/s². Eliminating time between x = (v₀ cosθ) t and y = (v₀ sinθ) t − ½ g t² gives the trajectory equation y = x tanθ − g x² / (2 v₀² cos²θ), a downward-opening parabola. We can compute range, maximum height, and time of flight from this equation. This worked example sits inside a unit on parametric equations and conic sections rather than physics.
subject: math
rationale: Topic resembles physics-projectile but section subject is math; SQL filter rejects.

section_content: In a coordinate plane we define a movement on the x-axis: an object starts at position 3, moves to position 8, then back to position 1. The signed change of position from start to end is −2 units. Distance travelled along the line is the sum of the absolute step lengths, 5 + 7 = 12 units. We use this as a one-dimensional warm-up for vector arithmetic and absolute value, before moving on to two-dimensional geometry. The number line picture is the standard way to visualise both quantities side by side and to feel the difference between scalar magnitude and signed displacement.
subject: math
rationale: Concept matches physics distance-vs-displacement entry but section subject is math.

section_content: Counting subsets of a finite set is a classical combinatorics question. For a set of n elements, every subset corresponds to a length-n string of 0s and 1s indicating which elements are in or out. So the total number of subsets is 2^n. For n = 3 there are 8, and we can arrange them in a partial order by inclusion: the empty set at the bottom, the full set at the top, layered subsets in between. Counting these layers gives the binomial coefficients C(3,0), C(3,1), C(3,2), C(3,3) = 1, 3, 3, 1, which sum to 8 by the binomial theorem.
subject: physics
rationale: Topic matches math power-set entry but section subject is physics; SQL filter rejects.

section_content: A stone tied to a string is whirled overhead in a horizontal circle of radius 0.8 m at a steady 4 m/s. Even though the speed is constant, the velocity is not — its direction is changing every instant. That continual change of direction is itself an acceleration, called centripetal acceleration, directed toward the centre of the circle and equal to v²/r = 16/0.8 = 20 m/s². The tension in the string supplies exactly this acceleration. If the string suddenly snaps, the stone keeps moving in a straight line tangent to the circle at the moment of release, not radially outward.
subject: physics
rationale: Uniform circular motion sits adjacent to projectile but is geometrically different; no library hit.

section_content: A block sits on a horizontal table; we attach a horizontal spring to it and pull it gently to one side. When released, the block oscillates back and forth across the equilibrium point. As long as the displacement stays small, the restoring force is proportional to the displacement: F = −kx. The motion is simple harmonic, with period T = 2π√(m/k). Plotting position against time gives a sinusoid — not a parabola — and plotting velocity against time gives another sinusoid shifted by a quarter period. The block is accelerating, but neither acceleration nor velocity is linear in time the way they are in uniformly accelerated motion.
subject: physics
rationale: SHM is adjacent to UAM kinematics graphs but the curves are sinusoidal, not linear/parabolic; no match.

section_content: Two distinct events happen on a number line. Event A is described by the rule "the value lands in the interval [2, 6]." Event B is described by "the value lands in the interval [4, 9]." The event "both A and B happen" corresponds to the overlap interval [4, 6]; the event "either A or B happens" corresponds to the combined interval [2, 9]. We treat intervals as sets of real numbers and apply set operations to them. Notice that interval intersection and union behave nicely on the real line because intervals are connected; for arbitrary subsets the geometry is messier.
subject: math
rationale: Set ops on intervals adjacent to general Venn-diagram entries; the intervals on a number line are not the discrete-set Venn picture in the library.

section_content: In a directed graph we draw a node for each element of the domain and a node for each element of the codomain, and we draw a directed edge for each input-output pair. A relation is any such collection of edges. The picture looks similar to the diagrams we use for functions, but a relation has no constraint that each domain node have exactly one outgoing edge — some can have several, others none at all. So although every function is a relation, not every relation is a function. The picture lets you spot which is which by counting outgoing edges per left-hand node.
subject: math
rationale: Adjacent to arrow-diagram entries but specifically about general relations rather than functions.

section_content: Take the set of natural numbers and define a relation: a is related to b if a divides b without remainder. This relation is reflexive (every number divides itself), antisymmetric (if a divides b and b divides a then a = b), and transitive (divides chains chain). Together those three properties make it a partial order. We can draw a layered diagram for the divisors of 12 with 1 at the bottom, primes 2 and 3 above, products like 4 and 6 above those, and 12 itself on top, with edges only between immediate cover pairs.
subject: math
rationale: Hasse-diagram-like topic but the entry in the library is specifically the power-set 3-element lattice, not divisibility.

section_content: A heavy ball is dropped from rest off the edge of a tall building. Air resistance is negligible, so the ball accelerates straight downward at 9.8 m/s². The path is a vertical line, not a curve — there is no horizontal motion at all. After 2 s the ball has fallen 19.6 m and is moving at 19.6 m/s. The motion sits inside the broader topic of free fall, but unlike a thrown object the trajectory has no shape worth sketching: it is just a downward arrow growing longer with time. The interesting graphs are height-vs-time and velocity-vs-time, not the spatial path.
subject: physics
rationale: Pure vertical drop is adjacent to projectile but the motion is not parabolic and there is no 2D trajectory to match the projectile entry.

section_content: On a hot summer day, suppose the people at a community pool are split into swimmers and the people at the same pool wearing sunglasses. We want to focus on the people who are doing both — swimming and wearing sunglasses. That smaller group is the slice where the two categories meet. Drawing the two categories as overlapping circles, the slice we want is the lens of overlap in the middle. Mathematically, this combination operation between two collections is called the meet, and it satisfies commutative and associative laws much like multiplication.
subject: math
rationale: "Meet" / overlap-of-categories is a synonym for set intersection; library entry should match.

section_content: The launch velocity of a thrown javelin can be split into two perpendicular legs. The leg that lies along the ground is found by multiplying the launch speed by the cosine of the launch angle. The leg pointing straight up is found by multiplying the launch speed by the sine of the launch angle. Together they sum vectorially back to the original launch arrow. This kind of right-triangle breakdown of a slanted vector into ground-level and vertical legs is the standard first step before applying kinematics to any angled-launch problem.
subject: physics
rationale: Velocity decomposition into horizontal/vertical components, paraphrased; library has it.

section_content: A small dataset on a number line will help us see what's going on. Suppose a beetle starts at the 0 mark, crawls to position 12, then doubles back to position 5. The total length its body covered along the line is 12 + 7 = 19 units. The straight-line offset from start to finish, however, is just +5 units. The two numbers usually disagree whenever the path bends or reverses. We use absolute path length when we care about effort or fuel; we use signed offset when we care only about where it ended up relative to where it started.
subject: physics
rationale: Same distance-vs-displacement concept paraphrased with a beetle; library has the curved-path entry.

section_content: Imagine a ball pitched straight upward into still air. As it ascends, it slows, freezes momentarily at the apex, and then descends, gaining speed in the opposite direction. Throughout the journey gravity is the only force acting, so the rate of speed change is constant downward. If we plot the ball's velocity against time, taking upward as positive, we see a single straight line crossing the time axis at the apex. The line never bends; only its sign flips at the moment of zero velocity, which is exactly when the ball is at peak altitude.
subject: physics
rationale: Free-fall v-t graph with sign change at apex, paraphrased.

section_content: Stack two operations: first cube the input, then add 7 to whatever you got. Feed in the number 2 and the cube box returns 8, then the add-7 box turns it into 15. We can package the two-step pipeline as a single composite operation. Drawing the data flow as boxes connected by arrows — input feeds the cube box, the cube box feeds the add-7 box, and the add-7 box emits the final answer — makes it visually obvious what "do this then that" means and why the order of the boxes matters.
subject: math
rationale: Composition pipeline (do g, then f) paraphrased without using the word composition; library has the f-after-g pipeline.

section_content: A scooter rider opens the throttle, holds it for 4 seconds, then closes it for the next 4 seconds. While the throttle is open her speed climbs at 2 m/s²; when it shuts she coasts and friction slows her at 0.5 m/s². The velocity-vs-time picture is a piecewise-linear graph with two distinct slopes meeting at a corner — first a steep upward segment, then a gentler downward one. This is two stages of uniformly accelerated motion stitched together at a kink. The library has clean single-segment exemplars but no piecewise composite of this kind.
subject: physics
rationale: Piecewise v-t with a corner is adjacent to single-segment UAM v-t entry but distinct in shape; no library match.

section_content: Suppose machine F maps a real number x to its square, and machine G maps a real number x to x + 1. We're interested in the operation "first square, then add 1." Feed 4 into F and you get 16; feed 16 into G and you get 17. We can short-circuit by writing the combined rule directly: take the input, square it, add 1. Drawing two boxes wired in series — input arrow into F, F's output arrow into G, G's output arrow out — reveals at a glance that the order F-then-G is what builds the new map.
subject: math
rationale: "First F, then G" is g-after-f composition; library entry exists for this direction specifically.

section_content: Consider the rule that maps each student in a class to the month they were born. Every student gets matched to exactly one month, but several students will share a month, and a few months will have no one assigned to them at all. So the rule is a function — every input has one output — but it's neither one-to-one nor onto. The picture is two columns with arrows fanning from the student column into the month column, several arrows piling onto popular months, and a few months left untouched. This is a generic function, not a perfect pairing.
subject: math
rationale: Adjacent to the bijective arrow-diagram entry but this function is many-to-one and not surjective; library has only the perfect-pairing entry.

section_content: Consider a survey: out of 50 students, 28 own a phone, 19 own a tablet, and 8 own neither. The students who own at least one of the two devices number 50 − 8 = 42. Using the principle that the size of the merged group equals the sum of each group minus the overlap, we get 28 + 19 − |both| = 42, so |both| = 5 students own both. Visualizing the merge as two overlapping circles — with one circle representing phone-owners, the other tablet-owners, and the surrounding rectangle representing all 50 students — makes the arithmetic feel natural.
subject: math
rationale: At-least-one-of-two = union; the diagram described is a Venn union; library has it.

section_content: Standing at the top of a 20 m cliff, a child throws a stone straight down at an initial speed of 5 m/s. We treat down as positive, so the initial velocity is +5 m/s and the acceleration due to gravity is +9.8 m/s². After 1.5 s the stone has fallen 5(1.5) + ½(9.8)(1.5)² ≈ 18.5 m and is moving at 5 + 9.8(1.5) = 19.7 m/s. To visualise both the height shrinking with time and the speed growing with time, students often want two synchronised graphs side by side: a downward-sloping height-vs-time curve and an upward-sloping velocity-vs-time line. Only the velocity-vs-time picture has a directly-matching exemplar in our visual library.
section_title: Stone Thrown Down from a Cliff
subject: physics
rationale: Section mentions two visual needs but library only has the v-t free-fall entry as a clean match.

section_content: Three sets A, B, and C sit inside a universe U, each pair overlapping with the others. The region we want is the small kite in the very middle where all three sets overlap simultaneously — every element that belongs to A and B and C at once. The picture is the classic three-circle Venn arrangement with seven distinct internal regions. The library has Venn diagrams for two-set operations (union, intersection, difference, complement), but the three-set picture with its central triple-overlap is a different image with more regions and a different geometry.
subject: math
rationale: Three-set Venn with triple overlap is adjacent to the two-set intersection entry but the visual is structurally different; no library match.

section_content: A toy car accelerates from rest at a constant 1.5 m/s² for 6 seconds. We can describe the same motion with three different graphs that capture three different quantities versus time. The acceleration is constant, so its graph is a flat horizontal line at 1.5. The velocity grows linearly from 0 to 9, so its graph is a straight line through the origin. The position grows quadratically from 0 to 27, so its graph is a parabolic arc opening upward. We focus this section on the position-time picture, which shows the parabolic shape of uniformly accelerated motion clearest.
subject: physics
rationale: Mentions three UAM graphs but anchors on the x-t parabola specifically; library has it.

section_content: To prove that the square root of 2 is irrational, suppose for contradiction that it equals p/q in lowest terms. Squaring both sides, 2 = p²/q², so p² = 2q². The right-hand side is even, so p² is even, hence p is even (since the square of an odd number is odd). Write p = 2k. Then 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k², hence q is also even. But p and q being both even contradicts our assumption that p/q was in lowest terms. The contradiction forces the conclusion: √2 cannot be written as a ratio of integers.
subject: math
rationale: Logical proof, no inherent visual need; LLM extractor should return [] or noisy needs that miss everything.

section_content: The principle of mathematical induction works in two stages. First, we verify the claim for the smallest natural number in scope — typically 1 or 0. Second, we assume the claim holds for some natural number k and use that to prove it holds for k + 1. If both stages succeed, the claim holds for every natural number from the base value upward, by an unbroken chain of implications. Induction is essentially a domino argument formalised: knock the first one over, ensure each one knocks the next, and the entire infinite line falls.
subject: math
rationale: Pure logical exposition; no concept-specific visual need that matches any library entry.

section_content: We say a function is increasing on an interval if, for every pair of points a and b in the interval with a < b, the function values satisfy f(a) < f(b). We say it is non-decreasing if the inequality is replaced with f(a) ≤ f(b). The two notions agree wherever the function is strictly monotonic but diverge whenever the function has a flat plateau — a non-decreasing function may sit at the same value across an interval, but a strictly increasing one may not. The distinction matters for inverse-function arguments later in the unit.
subject: math
rationale: Definitional, no concrete visual need; if extractor produces anything it shouldn't match a specific library entry.

section_content: Newton's laws of motion are not derived from anything more fundamental in classical mechanics; they are stated as axioms and then defended by the consistency of the predictions they generate. The first law asserts a body's tendency to keep doing what it's doing absent a net force. The second quantifies the relationship between force, mass, and acceleration. The third claims that forces always come in equal-and-opposite pairs across two bodies. Three short statements; the rest of mechanics is downstream of them. Discussing them at the axiom level is a verbal exercise; no specific image is essential here.
subject: physics
rationale: Verbal axiom-level discussion; no concept-specific visual need that matches a library entry.

section_content: In this lesson we examine a function from the integers to the integers defined by f(n) = n + 7. We can verify that this function never sends two different integers to the same value: if f(a) = f(b) then a + 7 = b + 7 hence a = b. We can also verify that every integer is hit: for any target m, the integer m − 7 is mapped onto m. So the function is one-to-one and onto. The traditional way to picture this is two columns of integer dots with arrows showing each input flying to its image.
subject: physics
rationale: Topic matches math bijection arrow-diagram entry but section subject is physics; SQL filter rejects.

section_content: A racecar enters a long straight at 40 m/s, holds that speed for 8 seconds, and then exits the straight still at 40 m/s. Throughout this stretch the velocity is constant, so the acceleration is zero, and the position grows linearly with time at the rate of 40 m/s. Plot velocity against time and you get a horizontal line at 40 — not a sloped line, because nothing is changing. The flatness of the v-t line is the visual signature of zero acceleration. This is the trivial limiting case of uniformly accelerated motion, with the slope set to zero.
subject: physics
rationale: Constant-velocity v-t graph is adjacent to UAM v-t entry but specifically the zero-acceleration case; library entry shows non-zero slope.

section_content: Three people stand around a table: Asha, Bilal, and Chitra. Their heights are 160 cm, 168 cm, and 155 cm respectively. We can list every possible pairing of one of them with one height value: Asha-160, Asha-168, Asha-155, Bilal-160, and so on. This 3-by-3 array is the Cartesian product of the people set and the height set. Most of those nine pairs do not actually occur in real life — only three of them do, the diagonal corresponding to who is actually that tall. We use this distinction between the full product and a chosen subset to motivate the next definition.
subject: math
rationale: Cartesian product is adjacent to function arrow-diagram territory but the library has no Cartesian-product entry.

section_content: A long-distance runner picks up speed for the first 30 seconds of a race and then settles into a steady cruising pace. Her position-vs-time graph is a smooth bowl-shaped curve at the start that gradually straightens out into a constant-slope diagonal once she stops accelerating. The transition is where the curvature dies away and the slope becomes constant. This kind of two-phase position graph (acceleration phase blending into uniform-velocity phase) is a generalisation of the strict UAM parabola — the parabola only covers the first phase. The library has clean strict-UAM exemplars but no transition graph.
subject: physics
rationale: Adjacent to UAM x-t parabola but the section graph is a parabola transitioning into a straight line; library entry is the strict pure parabola only.

section_content: As a tennis ball flies through the air after being struck, the steady downward pull of gravity changes only the up-and-down part of its motion; the sideways part keeps gliding at the launch speed because no horizontal force is acting. The ball's path through space, traced from racket to bounce, swoops up to a peak and back down again as a smooth curved arc. Sketch the swooping curve, label the strike point, the high point, and the bounce point, and you have everything needed to talk about how high it went, how long it stayed up, and how far it travelled.
subject: physics
rationale: Tennis-ball arc is a synonym for angled projectile trajectory; library entry is the 60-degree exemplar.

section_content: A small mass hangs at the end of a horizontal spring, displaced from its rest position and then released. It glides back toward equilibrium, overshoots, and oscillates back and forth indefinitely as long as friction is negligible. The position relative to the rest point traces out a perfect cosine curve in time: at the start it sits at the maximum amplitude, after one quarter of the period it crosses zero, after half a period it is at the negative maximum, and after a full period it has returned to where it began. The amplitude stays constant cycle after cycle and the time between identical states — the period — depends only on the mass and the spring stiffness, not on how far it was pulled to begin with.
section_title: Mass on a Spring Oscillating in Time
subject: physics
rationale: Section describes a cosine-in-time displacement trace for SHM; library has the displacement-vs-time exemplar at amplitude A and period T.

section_content: Two identical sound waves arrive at the same point in a room from speakers placed side by side. Because both speakers fire at exactly the same instant from the same source signal, the crests of the two waves line up — crest meets crest, trough meets trough — and the resulting pressure variation at the listener's ear is twice as loud as either wave alone. Drawing the two source waves on top of each other and the resulting sum on a third axis underneath shows the doubling clearly: the sum's crests are exactly above the source crests, and its amplitude is the simple addition of the two contributions. Whenever waves combine in this in-phase way, the result is amplification rather than cancellation.
subject: physics
rationale: Constructive interference of two in-phase waves with the doubled-amplitude sum traced on a separate axis; library has the three-stack constructive-superposition diagram.

section_content: A fire engine driving past a stationary pedestrian gives off a steady-pitch siren, but the pedestrian hears the pitch shift higher as the engine approaches and then drop sharply lower as it passes and recedes. The reason becomes clear once you sketch the wavefronts: each crest of the siren's sound is a sphere expanding outward from where the engine was at the instant that crest was emitted. As the engine drives forward, each new crest is emitted from a position slightly ahead of the previous one, so the crests bunch together in front of the engine and spread apart behind it. The pedestrian standing in front of the moving engine intercepts the bunched-up crests at a faster rate (higher frequency) and the same observer behind would intercept the stretched-apart crests more slowly (lower frequency).
subject: physics
rationale: Classical Doppler-effect explanation via moving emitter and bunched-vs-spread wavefronts; library has the moving-source-approaching diagram with compressed forward wavefronts.

section_content: A cyclist pedals along a flat road at a steady pace, covering the same amount of ground every second. We mark her position on a map every second and connect the readings on a graph. Time goes along the bottom axis, distance covered goes up the side. The points fall on a perfectly straight line that climbs through the origin: after one second she has gone five metres, after two seconds ten metres, after three seconds fifteen metres, and so on. The slope of the line — how steep it climbs — is exactly her speed in metres per second. A flatter line would mean a slower rider; a steeper line a faster one.
subject: physics
rationale: Linear distance-time graph for a constant-speed rider; library has the G9 d-t straight-line exemplar with slope-triangle annotation.

section_content: Imagine a strobe light flashing once every second above a small ball that has just been released down a smooth ramp. The ball was at rest at the top, then began rolling, and gravity steadily speeds it up. If we mark the ball's position at each flash and look at the row of marks left behind, the gaps between successive marks are not equal — they grow. Between the first and second flash there is a tiny gap; between the fifth and sixth flash a much larger gap. The growing-gap pattern is the visual signature of a body that is speeding up at a steady rate.
section_title: Strobe Trail of a Rolling Ball
subject: physics
rationale: Stroboscopic motion strip with progressively growing spacing — the canonical visual signature of uniform acceleration; library has the G9 accelerated motion-strip exemplar.

section_content: Two cars leave the same starting line at the same moment and reach the same finish line six seconds later. The first car cruises at a steady fifty kilometres per hour the whole way. The second car starts from rest, slowly picks up pace, and is going the fastest right at the moment it crosses the finish. To compare them we draw their distance-time graphs side by side, and their speed-time graphs side by side: one pair of plots shows a straight line and a curve; the other pair shows a flat horizontal line and a rising diagonal. Lined up next to each other, the difference between uniform and accelerated motion becomes obvious.
section_title: Two Cars, Same Finish, Different Stories
subject: physics
rationale: Side-by-side d-t and v-t plots comparing uniform and accelerated motion; library has the G9 comparison-grid exemplar.

section_content: In the early 1900s a famous tabletop experiment fired a stream of small positively-charged particles at a sheet of gold so thin that one could almost see through it. Most of the particles passed straight on as if the foil were not there at all, struck a phosphor screen behind, and produced a faint glow. A handful, however, came almost straight back toward the source — a result the researcher described as the most surprising thing he had ever seen, like a cannonball bouncing off tissue paper. Sketching the foil with the bombarding particles drawn as straight-through paths, occasional small deflections, and the rare wide-angle reflections lets us reason about what kind of structure the atom must have to produce that pattern.
section_title: Firing Particles at a Gold Sheet
subject: chemistry
rationale: Classic Rutherford gold-foil experiment with most α-particles passing through and rare back-scatter; library has the corresponding apparatus diagram with deflection paths.

section_content: After the s subshell, which is a single sphere, the next shape an electron can take on is a pair of opposing lobes — a kind of three-dimensional figure-eight pinched at the nucleus. There are three of these dumbbell shapes, perpendicular to one another and oriented along the three coordinate axes; together they make up a single subshell that can hold up to six electrons. To picture them, draw three sets of axes and on each set sketch a fat dumbbell aligned along one axis at a time. The three together fill space symmetrically around the nucleus.
subject: chemistry
rationale: Three perpendicular p-orbital dumbbells aligned along x, y, z axes; library has the canonical diagram with px, py, pz labels.

section_content: Electrons fill subshells in a specific order that is not just the simple counting order one through seven. Instead, the rule says: write the subshells out in a grid with the principal quantum number on rows and the subshell letter on columns, then sweep diagonally from upper-right toward lower-left, picking off subshells in that diagonal order. The first sweep gives 1s; the next gives 2s, then a longer one gives 2p and 3s; the next 3p and 4s; and so on. This produces the order one s, two s, two p, three s, three p, four s, three d, four p — which differs from the naïve grade-school sequence and predicts the structure of the periodic table itself.
section_title: The Diagonal Rule for Filling Subshells
subject: chemistry
rationale: Aufbau principle's diagonal-sweep rule with explicit subshell sequence 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p; library has the diagonal-arrow grid diagram.

section_content: Imagine slicing through a tiny soft blob from inside your skin and looking at the cross-section. You'd see a thin flexible outer skin holding everything together, a roundish dark patch off to one side that acts as the brain of the operation, several smaller bean-shaped structures scattered around that burn fuel to keep the place running, a network of squiggly tubes near the brain-patch with little dots dusted along them, and a stack of curved plates that wrap things up for delivery. Drawing all those parts in one picture with thin lines pointing from each part to its name on the side gives you a single chart you can come back to whenever someone mentions any of those names.
subject: biology
rationale: Description of an animal cell's major organelles (membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, ER with ribosomes, Golgi) with leader-line labels; library has the canonical labelled animal-cell diagram.

section_content: Zooming into one of the bean-shaped structures we mentioned earlier, you find that what looked like a smooth bean from the outside actually has two skins, and the inside skin is wrinkled into deep folds that stick into the centre. Those folds are not decorative — they massively increase the surface area where chemical work can happen. The inner space between the folds is where sugar gets combined with oxygen to release the energy currency the cell spends on everything else. Drawing the bean with its outer smooth wall, its scalloped inner folds, and a couple of energy-bursts emerging from one end captures the whole story of what this organelle is for.
subject: biology
rationale: Description of mitochondrion's outer membrane + folded inner membrane (cristae) + matrix + ATP production; library has the bean-shape diagram with cristae and ATP particles.

section_content: Living things come in a huge range of sizes, and so do the smallest pieces they're made of. A virus is hundreds of times smaller than a single bacterium; a bacterium is ten or twenty times smaller than the cells in your skin; a typical plant cell is about ten times bigger again; and a grain of sand on the beach is bigger still — visible to the eye without any help. To make sense of these jumps it's standard to lay them out along a single horizontal line where each step is ten times the previous one, with a marker for each kind of object pinned at its right size, and a band underneath showing which microscope (electron, light, or none) you'd need to see it.
section_title: How Big Are All the Tiny Things
subject: biology
rationale: Logarithmic size scale ranging from virus through bacterium, animal cell, plant cell, to grain of sand, with microscopy-bands underneath; library has the canonical biology size chart.

section_content: To make a small light come on we need three things connected in a closed loop. First, something that pushes — a battery, which acts like a tiny pump for the wires. Second, a thing-to-be-powered — a small bulb that glows when current flows through it. And third, a way to interrupt the loop on demand: a small lever or button that physically breaks the wire when off and bridges it when on. Drawing all three around a rectangular loop, with the pump on one edge, the lever on another edge, and the glowing thing on a third, captures the simplest possible electrical circuit. The fourth edge is plain wire connecting them.
subject: physics
rationale: Battery + switch + lamp in a rectangular closed loop — the canonical Hello-World circuit; library has the matching schematic with current arrow.

section_content: Two bulbs can be wired together in two different ways. In the first arrangement, the wire goes from the battery, through bulb A, through bulb B, and back to the battery — both bulbs sit on the same single wire path. If A breaks, B can no longer get current either, because the path is broken. In the second arrangement, the wire splits in two after leaving the battery; one branch passes through A, the other through B; the two branches rejoin before returning to the battery. Now if A breaks, B is still on its own loop and stays lit. Drawing the two arrangements side by side, with one bulb crossed out in each, makes the structural difference impossible to miss.
section_title: Two Ways to Wire Two Bulbs
subject: physics
rationale: Series-vs-parallel comparison with a broken bulb in each — the canonical pedagogical contrast; library has the side-by-side diagram with X-marked bulbs.

section_content: There's a famous tidy relationship between three quantities in any circuit: the push the battery applies, the rate at which charge flows, and the friction-like resistance the wire and components offer. The push equals the flow times the resistance — and from that single statement we can rearrange to get any one quantity in terms of the other two. A small triangle drawn with the push at the top and the flow next to the resistance at the bottom is the standard visual mnemonic: cover any letter with your finger and what's left is its formula. Doubling the push doubles the flow if resistance stays the same; doubling the resistance halves the flow if the push stays the same.
subject: physics
rationale: Ohm's law triangle mnemonic with V on top, I and R below — describes V = I·R and its rearrangements; library has the canonical triangle diagram.

section_content: All the chemical elements that exist can be lined up in a single chart with rows and columns. Each row contains elements that have the same number of electron shells; each column contains elements that share their outermost shell pattern and therefore behave chemically alike. The chart is wider than it is tall, with a tall pair of columns on the far left, a wide block of columns in the middle, and a smaller block of columns on the right. Cells are coloured by family — soft yellow for the column on the far left, lime for the next-to-last column, cyan for the very last column. A legend at the bottom translates each colour into a family name.
section_title: The Big Chart of All Elements
subject: chemistry
rationale: Periodic table arranged in periods (rows) and groups (columns) with cells colour-coded by family; library has the canonical G7 overview with the eight-category legend.

section_content: For each of the first twenty elements, draw a tiny atom: a small dot for the nucleus, then concentric rings for each shell of electrons, with little marks placed around each ring to count the electrons in that shell. Arrange the twenty miniatures in their proper grid positions — same column when the outermost ring has the same number of marks. Hydrogen sits alone at the top-left with one mark on one ring; helium goes top-right with two marks on one ring; lithium starts a new row with two marks on the inner ring and one on the outer; and so on through calcium with shells of two, eight, eight, two.
section_title: Twenty Tiny Atoms in a Grid
subject: chemistry
rationale: Mini Bohr-shell diagrams for first 20 elements arranged in periodic-table positions; library has exactly this layout (H through Ca, periods 1-4).

section_content: Some atoms grab shared electrons more strongly than others. Fluorine is the greediest grabber on the chart; cesium and francium are the weakest. Imagine colouring every cell on the periodic table by how strongly that element pulls — deep red for the strongest pullers, soft pink for moderate, almost-grey for the weakest, and uncoloured for the noble-gas column (which doesn't form bonds at all). The result is a heatmap with the deepest red concentrated in the upper-right corner of the chart, fading away to the lower-left.
subject: chemistry
rationale: Electronegativity heatmap with strongest pull in upper-right (fluorine) shading toward lower-left; library has the Pauling-scale colour-coded trend heatmap.

section_content: Drawing every single carbon and hydrogen in a long chain gets tedious quickly. Chemists shortcut this by replacing the chain with a simple zigzag line: each corner of the line is understood to be a carbon atom, the open ends of the line are understood to be carbon atoms too, and you don't write any of the hydrogens — they're filled in mentally based on each carbon needing four bonds total. To show the contrast, draw the same molecule three times: once with every atom written out, once as a string of CH₃-CH₂-CH₂-CH₃ symbols, and once as the zigzag.
section_title: Three Ways to Draw the Same Molecule
subject: chemistry
rationale: Comparison of full structural, condensed, and skeletal-zigzag depictions of butane; library has the canonical three-panel diagram.

section_content: Some molecules have a long backbone of single-bonded carbons; others have a slightly different arrangement where two of those carbons are joined by two parallel bonds instead of one. The double-bonded version is named with the suffix that ends in a soft sound rather than the hard one — and the position number tells you which two carbons share the doubled bond. To picture three of them: a two-carbon version with the doubled bond at the only available position; a three-carbon version with the doubled bond starting at the leftmost carbon; and a four-carbon version with the doubled bond between the second and third carbons.
section_title: Carbons That Share a Double Bond
subject: chemistry
rationale: Three alkene structures (ethene, propene, but-2-ene) differing in chain length and double-bond position; library has these three side-by-side.

section_content: To name an organic molecule systematically, follow the same five questions every time. First, what is the longest unbroken carbon chain — that gives you the parent name. Second, what side-branches stick off that chain — those are the substituents. Third, number the chain from whichever end gives those branches the smallest position numbers. Fourth, list the substituents alphabetically with their position numbers. Finally, swap the parent's last syllable for the suffix matching the highest-priority functional group present. Drawing this as a five-step decision tree, with each step in its own labelled card connected to the next by a downward arrow, lets you walk a student through the process visually.
subject: chemistry
rationale: IUPAC five-step naming flowchart with sequential numbered cards; library has the vertical numbered-card flowchart with arrows.

section_content: Pick a smooth curve drawn on a graph and choose a single point on it. The slope of the curve at that exact point — the rate at which it's rising or falling right there — is what we mean by the derivative. To approximate this slope, pick a second point a bit further along the curve and draw the straight line connecting the two; that line is what mathematicians call a chord cutting through the curve. As the second point slides closer to the first, the cutting line pivots and gets closer and closer to a single special line that just kisses the curve at the chosen point.
section_title: What the Slope of a Curve Means
subject: math
rationale: Description of tangent-as-limit-of-secants — chord pivoting toward kissing line as second point slides in; library has the canonical four-secant fan with shrinking Δx.

section_content: To differentiate a function of the form 'something raised to a power', there's a single quick recipe. Take whatever exponent the variable is being raised to, write it down as a multiplier in front, and then drop the exponent itself by exactly one. So x raised to the cube becomes three times x squared; x to the fifth becomes five x to the fourth; even x to a negative two becomes negative two times x to a negative three. Drawing this as a single highlighted equation card with the rule on top and four worked examples beneath makes it the kind of thing students can lock into memory in a minute.
section_title: A Quick Recipe for Differentiating Powers
subject: math
rationale: Power rule d/dx(x^n) = n·x^(n-1) with worked examples; library has the canonical formula card with four examples beneath.

section_content: A spherical balloon is being inflated by a pump that pushes air in at a constant rate of 5 cubic centimetres per second. As more air goes in the radius grows, but not steadily — when the balloon is small the radius shoots up quickly, and as it gets bigger the same volume of air spreads over a larger surface so the radius creeps up more slowly. The relationship between the rate of volume change and the rate of radius change comes from differentiating the volume formula V = (4/3)πr³, giving dV/dt = 4πr² · dr/dt and letting us solve for dr/dt at any specific radius.
section_title: How Fast Does the Balloon Get Bigger?
subject: math
rationale: Classic related-rates problem with balloon volume + radius and constant air-input rate; library has the three-balloon time-series with dV/dt → dr/dt walkthrough.

section_content: All the kinds of light we know about — the visible colours we see with our eyes, but also the radio waves carrying music to our cars, the warmth our skin feels from a heater, and the rays a dentist uses to image teeth — are members of one big family. Lay them out side by side along a single coloured strip ordered by wavelength: the longest at one end (radio, kilometres long), shrinking through microwave, infrared, the tiny visible-light slice, ultraviolet, X-rays, and finally gamma rays at the shortest end. The visible band is so narrow on this scale that it almost disappears.
section_title: All the Kinds of Light Are One Family
subject: physics
rationale: Description of the EM spectrum strip showing all bands ordered by wavelength with visible as a narrow slice; library has the canonical seven-band coloured strip.

section_content: Two completely independent things change about a sound. One is how often the air pressure rises and falls each second — that's what your brain interprets as 'higher' or 'lower'. The other is how big the rises and falls are — that's what you hear as 'louder' or 'quieter'. To make this concrete, draw four little wave traces side by side: one with fast wiggles and tall wiggles, one with fast wiggles but small wiggles, one with slow wiggles but tall wiggles, and one with slow wiggles and small wiggles. Each is labelled with the corresponding pitch-loudness combination.
subject: physics
rationale: Four-panel pitch-vs-loudness grid (fast/slow wiggles × tall/short wiggles); library has exactly this 2x2 panel layout.

section_content: Push a child's swing at random moments and not much happens. But push it once each time it returns to you, in time with its natural rhythm, and the height of each swing grows dramatically. The same effect appears in any oscillator that has a preferred wiggle-rate. Plotting the size of the response against the rate at which you're driving it gives a sharp peak right where the driving rate matches the oscillator's natural rate — and falls off rapidly on either side of that peak.
section_title: When Pushing in Time Makes Things Grow
subject: physics
rationale: Resonance amplitude curve peaking at f/f_natural = 1; library has the canonical bell-shaped curve with the swing-pushing analogy.
